title: Deep learning-based gait analysis predicts multisystem health phenotypes
desc: We developed a gait foundation model from three-dimensional skeletal motion data of 3,328 deeply phenotyped adults, recorded using a depth camera during five motor tasks. Embeddings significantly predicted 1,887 of 3,210 phenotypic targets and provided predictive gains across all 18 body systems in men and 17 out of 18 in women, while also improving prediction of clinical diagnoses and medication use.

title: Multimodal cell foundation models require synergistic integration beyond alignment
desc: Integrating measurements across modalities and scales into unified quantitative frameworks of cellular function is a central goal in computational biology. Although powerful unimodal foundation models exist, the scarcity of large-scale paired data limits joint multimodal training. This constraint favours compositional foundation models, which fuse frozen unimodal experts through a learned interface. However, it remains unclear when such fusion provides task-relevant information beyond the strongest unimodal representation rather than merely aggregating redundant signal. Here we introduce Synergistic Information Score, a metric grounded in partial information decomposition that quantifies information gain arising only from cross-modal interactions. Extending theory from self-supervised learning, we show that standard alignment-based objectives with frozen encoders collapse to detect linear redundancies, which constrains their ability to capture nonlinear synergistic states. This distinction is especially important for tasks that connect tissue morphology with gene expression. Benchmarking ten fusion methods on spatial transcriptomics datasets, we demonstrate that tasks dominated by linear redundancies are well served by unimodal baselines, whereas complex niche definitions benefit from synergy-aware integration. Finally, we perform a scaling analysis and show that fine-tuning a dominant unimodal expert is the most sample-efficient strategy for standard tasks. Together, these results suggest that progress in multimodal modelling of cellular state requires shifting from alignment-based objectives to synergy-driven integration that exploits complementary cross-modal signal. Richter et al. show that simply aligning different types of biological data does not fully integrate them, revealing when data repeat the same information and, conversely, when they provide complementary insights.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Pediatric Hospital Medicine: Foundations, Clinical Applications, and Emerging Case Uses.
desc: [Pediatric annals] Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming health care and has important implications for pediatric hospital medicine. Advances in machine learning and large language models have enabled applications that support patient care in the areas of clinical documentation, decision making, and prognostic modeling. Pediatric AI systems leverage diverse data sources, including electronic health records, medical imaging, physiologic monitoring, wearable devices, and genomic data. Current applications include AI-powered scribes, chart summarization, clinical decision support, prediction of sepsis and clinical deterioration, precision pharmacotherapy, rare disease diagnosis, and mental health interventions. These technologies have demonstrated potential to reduce clinician workload, enhance diagnostic accuracy, and facilitate earlier therapeutic interventions. However, significant challenges remain, including limited and heterogeneous pediatric datasets by virtue of age and developmental characteristics in children, bias, privacy concerns, lack of representativeness, and the need for rigorous validation and oversight. As AI adoption expands, pediatric hospitalists require foundational knowledge of AI principles and limitations to ensure safe, equitable, and effective implementation. With appropriate governance and multidisciplinary collaboration, AI has the potential to improve pediatric inpatient outcomes and health care delivery.

title: Static Recovery Is Not Dynamic Stability: Dynamics-Aware Benchmarking of Protein Motif Scaffolding
desc: Protein motif scaffolding benchmarks assess whether generative models can build scaffolds around functionally important residues. Their conclusions depend on which motifs are tested and which criteria define success. Existing benchmarks typically use small hand-curated motif sets and static refolding criteria, but protein function often depends on conformational ensembles and transitions. Here, we address both benchmark scope and success criteria. We introduce BILBY-PRO, a systematically derived benchmark of structurally conserved functional motifs from PROSITE-linked experimental structures, comprising 220 cases from 174 PROSITE motif-pattern entries. Evaluating six recent scaffold-generation models reveals distinct patterns in target coverage and unique-solution yield: RFDiffusion and Proteina solve more targets, whereas ESM3 produces more unique successful scaffolds on the targets it solves. We further introduce BILBY-MD, a reference-based all-atom molecular dynamics evaluation framework. Applied to statically solved designs from the original MotifBench benchmark, it compares motif drift, scaffold drift, motif-contact preservation, and motif-dihedral free-energy landscapes against reference simulations. Of 55 statically solved model-problem pairs, 31 satisfy our MD-supported criterion and only 8 pass all checks. Compact, self-contained motifs are often MD-supported, whereas interface-like or context-dependent motifs fail more frequently. Static refolding success therefore provides useful evidence of local motif recovery but does not establish dynamical fidelity of the full scaffold. BILBY highlights three complementary axes of motif-scaffolding evaluation: target coverage, unique-solution yield, and MD-supported dynamical fidelity.

title: Randomized Trial Protocol: Head-to-Head Comparison of Two Ambient Artificial Intelligence Documentation Tools on Clinician Usability
desc: Abstract Background: Ambient AI documentation reduces documentation burden and electronic health record (EHR) time for ambulatory clinicians. Newer features also queue orders and offer some level of coding support for clinician review. This study compares two commercial products deployed at UCLA Health. Objective: To compare Nabla and Epic Systems, Inc. ambient AI solution among ambulatory clinicians at UCLA Health on usability, documentation burden, perceived note quality, adoption, EHR time and productivity, clinician-reported experience with order queueing and coding support, coding and billing patterns and integrity, work productivity, and patient-reported communication experience. Methods: Two-arm parallel-group randomized trial, 1:1, among 374 ambulatory clinicians at a single academic health system who hold an active license for a standalone ambient application (Nabla). Randomization is covariate-constrained where cohort size permits, balancing age, sex, half-day clinic sessions, specialty group, and baseline System Usability Scale (SUS) score. Intervention runs 11/9/2026 to 1/17/2027, with the first four weeks as lead-in. The primary outcome is SUS score at follow-up, compared between arms. Analysis is by intention-to-treat using mixed-effects models. Ethics and dissemination: Determined exempt by the UCLA Institutional Review Board (IRB-26-2147). Survey completion indicates consent. No patient-level data are collected. Findings will directly inform operational decision making and will be published regardless of direction.

title: AI in the Clinical Documentation Loop: Effects of LLM-Induced Note Bloat and Diagnostic Overcall on Downstream LLMs
desc: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to process medical records for healthcare tasks such as clinical documentation. Because these tools also generate documentation, the relationship is now bidirectional: models both read from and write to the record. Understanding how LLMs behave when reading records that already contain LLM-authored content is therefore critical for their safe deployment. In this study, we examine how LLM-authored content in the medical record affects downstream LLMs that read the same record. We consider two types of LLM-induced artifacts: bloat, in which LLM-generated summaries accumulate in the record and change the length and provenance of its content over time; and distortion, in which LLMs subtly alter clinical findings rather than fabricating facts outright. As a case of distortion, we study diagnostic overcall (documenting an unconfirmed differential diagnosis in the record) and test whether it propagates to the reader LLM's output. Across seven reader models from four families, we find evidence of both effects. First, LLM-generated summary notes modestly but consistently degraded downstream hospital-course generation compared with copy-forward and templated text of matched length. Second, injected overcalls reappeared in downstream outputs at rates that varied by reader model, without detectable changes in standard quality metrics. These findings show the need to monitor AI-generated content in medical records and to account for it when those records are later processed by AI.

title: AOPTK: Open-Source Software for AI-Assisted Toxicological Literature Analysis
desc: Motivation: Toxicologists today face a challenge: although vast amounts of data describing how chemicals affect human health are available across scientific publications and regulatory reports, much of this information remains underutilized because extracting and interpreting evidence across thousands of studies is impractical to perform manually. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly in large language models (LLMs), provide new opportunities to automate toxicological literature analysis. Results: Herein, we present the Adverse Outcome Pathway Toolkit (AOPTK), an open-source Python package for AI-enhanced analysis of toxicological and biomedical literature. AOPTK supports (i) automated literature retrieval from databases such as PubMed Central and Europe PMC, (ii) direct processing of full-text articles in PDF format, and (iii) LLM-assisted analysis tools to identify chemicals and extract their relationships to biological effects under user-defined conditions. We demonstrate its utilities through a case-study identifying potential non-genotoxic carcinogens based on their ability to inhibit gap junction intercellular communication (GJIC). The LLM-enhanced analysis achieves 81% agreement with an expert-curated inhibitor list and 95% accuracy in predicting inhibition versus no inhibition when analysing the same subset of 86 publications. Automated retrieval and analysis of 1 124 publications from PubMed Central further demonstrated the feasibility of applying AOPTK to large-scale literature analyses. Availability: The package is developed open source on GitHub, disseminated through PyPI and Bioconda and releases are archived on Zenodo. Individual tools are available in the Galaxy platform for accessible data analysis with user-friendly, findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable (FAIR) and end-to-end workflows provided via WorkflowHub. The tools are available on usegalaxy.eu and usegalaxy.cz and are developed open source on GitHub.

Hemodynamic effects of semaglutide in individuals with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and obesity: a placebo-controlled randomized clinical trial
desc: As presented at the 2026 American Heart Association Scientific Sessions, in a placebo-controlled randomized clinical trial, semaglutide significantly improved pulmonary artery wedge pressure and other hemodynamic parameters during low-intensity exercise in individuals with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and obesity. The glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist semaglutide improves symptoms in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) through unclear mechanisms. Here, in this double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, we randomly assigned 81 patients (47 women) with HFpEF and obesity to semaglutide (2.4 mg weekly) or placebo for 52 weeks. The primary outcome was the change in invasively measured pulmonary artery wedge pressure (PAWP), a direct measure of cardiac congestion, during low-intensity exercise. Additional mechanistic outcomes included other hemodynamic measures and hemodynamic HFpEF remission (defined as normal PAWP under conditions of both rest and exercise at 52 weeks). At baseline, PAWP was 17.5 ± 4.3 mmHg at rest and 31.7 ± 5.2 mmHg during exercise. After 52 weeks, the mean change in PAWP during exercise was −9.8 (95% confidence interval (CI): −11.3 to −8.2) mmHg with semaglutide and +0.9 (95% CI: −1.3 to 3.0) mmHg with placebo (estimated difference, −10.6 mmHg; 95% CI: −13.3 to −8.0; P < 0.0001). As compared to placebo, semaglutide also decreased resting PAWP (estimated difference, −7.1 mmHg; 95% CI: −9.8 to −4.4; P < 0.0001), and semaglutide-treated patients were more likely to experience hemodynamic remission (53.7% versus 7.4%, odds ratio = 14.1, 95% CI: 3.0−134.6, P < 0.001). The results from this trial indicate that, in patients with HFpEF and obesity, treatment with semaglutide reduced left heart filling pressures during exercise and at rest and was associated with hemodynamic HFpEF remission in over half of treated patients. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05371496 .

title: Artificial Intelligence in Pediatric Hospital Medicine: Governance, Ethics, Education, Research, and the Future Workforce.
desc: [Pediatric annals] Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing pediatric inpatient care, extending beyond clinical applications to many areas of health care delivery, medical education, and research. Studies suggest that families are receptive to AI-assisted care if transparency, human oversight, and shared decision making are maintained. Effective governance is necessary to address concerns related to accountability, privacy, regulatory gaps, postdeployment monitoring, and equitable implementation. Algorithmic bias, data representativeness, informed consent, and the potential for AI to exacerbate health care disparities pose new ethical concerns. Explainable AI may improve transparency, trust, and acceptance by clinicians through making AI-generated recommendations more understandable. AI can also transform medical education through personalized learning, simulation, and clinical decision support, while requiring new competencies in AI literacy. AI offers opportunities to expedite clinical trials and data analysis but requires pediatric-specific frameworks to address age-related bias and emphasize ethical use of pediatric data in research. Responsible implementation, strong oversight, multidisciplinary collaboration, and continued clinician leadership will be essential to realizing AI's potential while safeguarding the welfare of pediatric patients and their families.

title: AI-Based Tools for Stroke Diagnosis, Treatment and Outcome Prediction: a Multicentre Prospective Observational Study
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Hospital Universitari Vall d'Hebron Research Institute; conditions: Stroke, Ischemic Stroke, Intracerebral Hemorrhage, Transient Ischemic Attack, Atrial Fibrillation; type: OBSERVATIONAL; enrollment: 10000; status: RECRUITING] Stroke is a leading cause of death and adult disability. Stroke care is still limited by fragmented care pathways, non-standardised diagnostic work-up and follow-up, and local, non-interoperable data systems across the pre-hospital, in-hospital and post-hospital settings. UMBRELLA-P is a multicentre, prospective, observational study in 7 university hospitals in 6 European countries (Spain, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands, Germany and Switzerland). Adults with clinically suspected acute stroke or transient ischemic attack (TIA) are managed according to standard of care. Routine clinical, imaging, laboratory, ECG and patient-reported data are collected, pseudonymised, stored on a dedicated server at each hospital and harmonised to the OMOP Common Data Model. The harmonised data form a federated real-world data platform (U-Platform). On this platform, artificial intelligence (AI) models are trained and validated through federated learning, so that no patient data leave the participating sites. The models aim to predict short- and long-term outcomes, reduce time to treatment, and support diagnosis, triage, discharge, follow-up and secondary prevention. Five clinical sub-studies address pre-hospital triage, fast track to reperfusion, emergent intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) management, TIA/minor stroke, and cardiac evaluation with blood biomarkers. The study is observational. The outputs of the AI models are used for research only and will not influence clinical decisions. Participants are followed for up to 12 months.

title: Multi-Agent Generative Artificial Intelligence for Transfusion Reaction Feature Extraction
desc: BACKGROUND: Many transfusion reactions are not reported to hemovigilance systems, and the features needed to recognize them are often documented only in free-text clinical notes. We sought to develop and evaluate an open-source, multi-agent artificial intelligence (AI) pipeline to extract transfusion reaction features defined by the National Healthcare Safety Network (NHSN) Hemovigilance Module from clinical notes. METHODS: We curated 181 features from the NHSN protocol and developed a multi-stage pipeline that extracted features, their timing, and clinical details from free-text notes. Three open-weight large language models (Qwen 3.6-27B, GPT-OSS-120B, and Kimi K3) were applied to 50 notes from expert-written scenarios, published case reports, and MIMIC-IV discharge summaries. Two physicians independently evaluated every model output in a blinded interface. The primary analysis was restricted to feature occurrences with concordant physician assessments. RESULTS: Physicians agreed on 1,201 of 1,343 co-rated feature occurrences (89.4%; Krippendorff's alpha 0.73). Precision was above 0.98 for all models. Sensitivity was 0.774 (95% CI 0.745-0.800) for Kimi K3, 0.636 (0.604-0.667) for GPT-OSS-120B, and 0.624 (0.593-0.655) for Qwen 3.6-27B, and specificity ranged from 0.952 to 0.991. Omissions accounted for more than 94% of false negatives. Timing and clinical details were judged supported or reasonable in more than 92% and 97% of assessments, respectively. Results were consistent across note sources and in analyses including discordant assessments. CONCLUSION: Multi-agent AI pipelines provide a feasible method for extracting transfusion reaction signals from clinical notes with high precision. Our work may have applications in active hemovigilance, reaction classification, and big data research.

title: Can General-Purpose Generative AI Supply Training Data for Medical Vision Models? A Multimodal Retrospective Study
desc: Background: Well-annotated, diverse medical imaging datasets remain a major constraint for vision-based medical AI. We evaluated Nano Banana, a general-purpose image generation and editing model, as a source of synthetic medical images for model training, subgroup augmentation, and model auditing. Methods: In this retrospective study across four imaging modalities, chest radiography, fundus photography, and CT models were trained only on synthetic images and externally validated on real-world data against real-data-trained models. Carotid ultrasound models were trained on a private Human Phenotype Project cohort (aged 40-75 years) with and without synthetic augmentation. Clinicians rated image plausibility. Evaluation used AUROC, AUPR, calibration, and decision curve analysis. Findings: Synthetic-only models achieved AUROCs of 0.877 (95% CI 0.843-0.910) for pneumonia (n=14863), 0.963 (0.948-0.975) for retinal detachment (n=1149), and 0.711 (0.600-0.823) for renal calculus (n=4122), comparable to real-data-trained models, but their calibration and net benefit were not consistently more favorable. With mixed synthetic-real training, a carotid ultrasound model produced an ordinal vascular age index that stratified 633 external subjects into subgroups differing in BMI and glucose (both p<0.01), linking vascular aging to cardiometabolic health. To stress-test shortcut learning, editing a moderate tessellated pattern into fundus photographs reduced the true-class probability for central serous chorioretinopathy from 0.996 to 0.822. Clinician-guided editing raised low-quality CT plausibility from 3.10/5 to 4.30/5. Interpretation: Synthetic data can complement real data in model training, subgroup representation, and model testing via controlled editing, but its clinical value should be assessed with calibration, decision curve analysis, and clinician review, not discrimination alone.

title: Leave-One-Out-Cross-Validation Based Machine Learning Algorithms for Efficient, Scalable, and Robust Prediction of Artemisinin Resistance in Plasmodium falciparum Kelch13 mutants.
desc: Emerging Plasmodium falciparum resistance to frontline artemisinin (ART) derivatives threatens global malaria control efforts. Current protocols assigning ART-sensitive (ART-S) or -resistant (ART-R) phenotypes to parasite strains with Kelch13 (K13) mutations remain time-intensive for real-time surveillance. Ring-survival assay (RSA), an ex vivo gold standard mandates laboratory-adaptation under culture conditions and frequently does not replicate clinical ART-responsiveness, thereby limiting its utility for rapidly triaging newly emerging K13 variants. In contrast, advent of artificial intelligence (AI)-derived models hold potential to screen >100 K13 variants within hours, enabling rapid near-real-time prediction of ART-S/R. Here, we engineered a panel of forty representative K13 variants by computing their relative deviations from wild-type K13 across ten physicochemical and structural descriptors, yielding a compact feature set which captures mutation-induced perturbations in folding, stability, and solvent exposure. These can be further utilized to train and validate AI classifier to predict resistance.

An ulcerative colitis taxonomy defined by individual patient-reported response trajectories
desc: An analysis of patient-reported trajectories of response to vedolizumab in ulcerative colitis defines disease endotypes and identifies vascular inflammation as a potential resistance mechanism. A barrier to precision medicine for ulcerative colitis (UC) is the inability to predict and mechanistically explain treatment responses. Using patient-reported outcomes (PROs) from a phase 3b comparative trial of 768 participants, we identified four distinct patient response-trajectory groups for vedolizumab (anti-integrin) and adalimumab (antitumor necrosis factor). Validation in a second phase 3 trial of 576 participants linked PRO-defined vedolizumab trajectories to long-term disease complications. Bulk, single cell, and spatial transcriptomics and proteomics identified vascular inflammation as associated with vedolizumab nonresponse through interactions between SPP1^+ macrophages and endothelial cells. In two separate real-world cohorts of 4,981 and 3,854 patients with UC, concomitant use of renin–angiotensin system inhibitors (modulators of vascular inflammation) was associated with reduced long-term complications for vedolizumab but not anticytokine therapies. These findings define a response-trajectory-based taxonomy that requires prospective validation for clinical utility and applications for selecting vedolizumab combination therapy in UC.

title: Predictive Analytics and Workflow Automation to Reduce Administrative Burden and Clinician Burnout in United States Clinical Settings: A Systematic Review.
source: PubMed · Advances in health information science and practice
desc: [Advances in health information science and practice] Electronic health record (EHR)-related administrative burden remains a frequently cited contributor to clinician burnout in the United States. Although digital systems were implemented to improve quality, safety, and care coordination, expanded documentation requirements, inbox messaging, and regulatory reporting have increased clerical workload. Traditional interruptive clinical decision support tools may further increase cognitive demands through alert fatigue and workflow disruption. Health systems have increasingly adopted predictive analytics and workflow-integrated automation, including ambient artificial intelligence (AI) documentation, inbox prioritization, and audit log-based workflow monitoring. However, their effects on operational efficiency and clinician well-being remain uncertain. This review examined clinician-facing interventions in US clinical settings and their impact on documentation workload, operational efficiency, and burnout-related outcomes. A systematic review guided by Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses was conducted using PubMed, CINAHL, and Embase. The search included English-language studies published between January 1, 2019, and December 31, 2025, with an updated search capturing eligible early online publications through 2026. Eligible studies evaluated clinician-facing predictive analytics or workflow automation in US clinical settings and reported measurable outcomes, including documentation time, after-hours EHR use, alert burden, cognitive task load, productivity, or validated burnout measures. Findings were synthesized narratively because interventions and outcome measures varied. Of 520 records identified, 173 unique records were screened; 24 (13.9%) underwent full-text review, and 7 of 24 (29.2%) met inclusion criteria. Ambient AI documentation platforms were associated with approximately 10%-30% reductions in documentation time, although findings on after-hours EHR activity varied. Several multisite implementations reported improvements in validated burnout measures and cognitive task load. AI-driven inbox prioritization reduced message review time, while audit log-based clinical decision support monitoring identified changes in EHR activity patterns following intervention. title: Automated MRI-Based Segmentation of the Cranio-Cervical Venous System Using a Dedicated Deep Learning Pipeline
desc: PURPOSE To develop an automated magnetic resonance imaging based segmentation pipeline for the cranio-cervical venous system (CCVS), a complex anatomical network for which no dedicated segmentation tool is currently available. MATERIALS AND METHODS A retrospective single-center cohort of 194 contrast-enhanced cranio-cervical MRI examinations acquired between 2019 and 2024 was used. Manual reference segmentations were performed on 50 examinations using 3D Slicer. A nnU-Net v2-based segmentation model was trained through an iterative process combining automatic segmentation, manual correction, and retraining. Segmentation performance was assessed using the Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC). The complete processing pipeline was integrated into an open-source software application, VenousNetworkAnalyzer (VNA). RESULTS The final model achieved a mean DSC of 0.94 (95% CI, 0.93-0.95) in five-fold cross-validation on 106 examinations with manual reference segmentations. Iterative optimization progressively reduced manual processing time from approximately 10 hours of fully manual segmentation to less than 10 minutes of manual correction per patient. Application of the final model to the entire cohort enabled the generation of patient-specific three-dimensional reconstructions of the cranio-cervical venous system. The segmentation workflow was successfully integrated into the VNA software environment, allowing automated processing and visualization of MRI datasets. CONCLUSION This study demonstrates the feasibility of automated segmentation of the cranio-cervical venous system from contrast-enhanced MRI using a dedicated deep-learning pipeline. The resulting reduction in processing time and integration into an open-source software platform provide a foundation for future large-scale anatomical studies of cranio-cervical venous draina

title: NanoNet: Ultra-Lightweight Network for MRI Brain Tumor Classification toward Edge AI
desc: Automated brain tumor classification from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can support accessible medical image analysis, but conventional deep learning models often exceed the resource budgets of highly constrained edge-AI platforms. We present NanoNet, an ultra-lightweight convolutional neural network designed for resourceconstrained MRI classification and motivated by future edge-AI applications. Inspired by MobileNetV2, NanoNet substantially reduces network depth, channel capacity, expansion ratios, and final feature dimensionality, resulting in only five inverted residual blocks and 8,132 parameters. We further investigate dependency-aware structured pruning, knowledge distillation, and INT8 quantization-aware training for additional compression. Experiments on the BRISC 2025 benchmark show that NanoNet achieves 92.80% accuracy and 92.97% macro F1 with 8,132 parameters and 10.498 MFLOPs. Across three compression seeds, it exceeds the mean accuracy of 70%-pruned MobileNetV2 by 5.20 percentage points while using 60.2% fewer parameters and 9.8% less computation. Converted INT8 NanoNet achieves 89.70% accuracy and 90.22% macro F1 across three QAT seeds. Earlier TensorFlow Lite measurements indicate 27.7 KB of baseline model storage, motivating future edge-AI deployment.

title: MELD: Mutation Effect Learning through Differential embeddings
desc: We introduce MELD (Mutation Effect Learning through Differential Embeddings), a compact model for predicting the functional consequences of single nucleotide variants (SNVs) by training directly on the wild-type (WT) versus mutant differential. Interpreting SNVs is central to clinical genomics, yet experimental characterization cannot scale to millions of observed variants. Leading sequence-to-function models (Enformer, Borzoi, AlphaGenome) are trained on absolute genomic tracks and score variants post hoc through in-silico mutagenesis (ISM), so the WT-mutant difference never enters the training loss. MELD instead places the logit difference {Delta}z = zmut - zwt inside the supervised objective. It combines a shared CNN-Transformer encoder, a mutant-specific mutation-mask boost, multiscale mutation-centered pooling, and a learned adaptive amplification factor . On ClinVar (1.57M variants), MELD (1.9M parameters) reached an AUROC of 0.986 versus 0.800 for a same-data, same-backbone ISM baseline, with ablations confirming the contribution of each component. On a shared benchmark, it outperformed frozen foundation models with 3-1,300x more parameters (AUROC 0.967 vs. 0.924 for AlphaGenome and 0.936 for Nucleotide Transformer). With only 50, 000 training variants, it exceeded the ISM baseline trained on all 1.48M (AUROC 0.903 vs. 0.796) variants. On BRCA1 saturation genome editing, frozen MELD achieved a Spearman {rho} of 0.42, above Borzoi (0.40), and ClinVar transfer raised it to 0.45. These results demonstrate that direct differential supervision is a compact, data-efficient alternative to post-hoc ISM scoring with substantially larger pretrained models.

Resistance exercise to attenuate lean mass loss during tirzepatide therapy for obesity: a randomized controlled trial
desc: Participants undergoing resistance exercise while receiving tirzepatide lost less lean mass than participants receiving tirzepatide alone. Incretin mimetics as obesity therapy induce substantial weight and fat loss but also decrease lean soft tissue mass, possibly impairing skeletal muscle function. Here, in this two-arm randomized controlled trial of adding resistance exercise (REx) to tirzepatide (T), 120 adults with overweight or obesity were treated with tirzepatide and randomized to thrice-weekly resistance exercise training or usual activities for 40 weeks. Tirzepatide was safe, and most participants tolerated up-titration to 15 mg weekly. Adherence to resistance exercise was 91%. Weight loss achieved was similar (T = −22.61 kg, T+REx = −22.28 kg, P = 0.694). For primary outcomes, loss of total fat mass was similar (T = −17.19 kg, T+REx = −17.98 kg, P = 0.700; between-group difference = −0.77 kg, 95% confidence interval (CI): −2.14 kg to 0.60 kg), but resistance exercise reduced loss of total lean soft tissue mass (T = −4.67 kg, T+REx = −3.57 kg, P < 0.001; between-group difference = 1.09 kg, 95% CI: 0.43−1.75 kg). Upper and lower body muscle strength decreased with tirzepatide (bench press −4.09 kg, lat pulldown −4.42 kg, knee extension −4.42 kg) but increased with T+REx (+4.68 kg, +8.58 kg, +5.88 kg, respectively, all P < 0.001 versus tirzepatide). In conclusion, resistance exercise training attenuated loss of total lean soft tissue mass, representing an effective adjunct to tirzepatide anti-obesity therapy. title: Artificial intelligence for cerebrovascular digital subtraction angiography: methods, evidence, and challenges.
source: PubMed · Physics in medicine and biology
desc: [Physics in medicine and biology] Cerebrovascular diseases remain a major cause of mortality and long-term disability worldwide. Digital subtraction angiography (DSA) provides high-spatiotemporal-resolution visualization of cerebrovascular anatomy and contrast-agent dynamics and plays an important role in diagnosis, interventional treatment planning, and treatment assessment. Artificial intelligence (AI) has increasingly been applied to cerebrovascular DSA, yet the available evidence is distributed across diverse imaging settings, technical tasks, datasets, and validation strategies. This structured topical review provides a DSA-centered overview of AI-assisted cerebrovascular image analysis across 2D DSA, three-dimensional rotational angiography, and four-dimensional DSA. Literature from Web of Science Core Collection and major engineering databases was screened at title, abstract, and full-text levels using predefined eligibility criteria. The literature is organized around six interconnected tasks: image preprocessing, vessel and lesion segmentation, image registration, reconstruction and generation, disease diagnosis and detection, and hemodynamic analysis. Representative conventional and learning-based methods are reviewed together with their datasets, evaluation metrics, validation designs, and available data or code resources, with particular attention to the strength and limitations of the supporting evidence. Recent studies demonstrate increasing use of spatiotemporal modeling, deep learning, and image-generation techniques, but clinical translation remains constrained by small or single-center datasets, heterogeneous acquisition protocols and evaluation practices, limited external and prospective validation, model interpretability, and deployment requirements. Future work should emphasize acquisition-aware and physics-informed modeling, multicenter and privacy-preserving collaboration, clinically meaningful validation, and closer integration with neurointerventional workflows. By linking methodological developments with their supporting evidence and translational challenges, this review aims to support the development of more robust and clinically applicable AI methods for cerebrovascular DSA.

title: BioLT: Streaming Biosignal Modeling
desc: Clinical biosignals such as ECG, PPG, and EEG are increasingly acquired as hours-long streams from bedside monitors and wearables, yet existing analysis pipelines almost universally operate on isolated short windows of around 10 seconds and cannot process the long, irregular, frequently interrupted signals. We introduce BioLT, a streaming decoder-only framework for long-context biosignal modeling that turns any window-level feature extractor or pretrained biosignal foundation model into a streaming model. BioLT combines (i) a discontinuity-aware encoding that exposes the inter-window elapsed time as an explicit input channel, so that the decoder can learn to model these gaps as clinically meaningful information, and (ii) a fixed-size compressed memory bank supervised with cumulative summary statistics, which keeps both training and inference linear in the recording length while preserving long-range context. We evaluate on CPSC-2021, VitalDB, MC-MED, and CHB-MIT for arrhythmia, sepsis, and seizure detection and for forecasting up to 20 minutes ahead, using domain features and embeddings from six biosignal foundation models. Across 21 dataset-feature settings, BioLT achieves the highest detection AUROC in 15 and the highest 20-minute forecasting AUROC in 13 settings, and shows consistent performance gains over state-of-the-art snapshot foundation-model embeddings. These highlight the importance of modeling how streaming biosignal representations evolve over time, beyond improving window-level representations alone.

title: Distinguishing Extraction Failures and Clinical Discordance with LLM Uncertainty on Radiology Reports
desc: Large language models (LLMs) can structure clinical datasets, but extraction error must be distinguished from discordance in the underlying data. From a real-world cohort of 1{,}045 patients undergoing coronary CT angiography (CCTA), we evaluated whether LLM uncertainty during vessel-level coronary artery disease (CAD) stenosis extraction could identify extraction failure and clinical discordance. References were expert CCTA annotations (253 patients) and subsequent invasive coronary angiography (ICA; 729 patients). We quantify extraction failure as disagreement between stenosis severity in LLM extracted versus expert annotations, and clinical discordance as disagreement in stenosis severity between CCTA and subsequent ICA. Stenosis Margin, selected from ten candidate measures, was used to quantify LLM uncertainty, and generalized estimating equation logistic regression and AUC evaluated its association and incremental discrimination for each failure mode. LLM uncertainty was strongly associated with extraction failure (adjusted OR 4.15 [95% CI 2.57--6.69], $P<0.001$) and substantially improved discrimination beyond LLM-extracted CCTA stenosis severity alone (AUC 0.81 to 0.86; $Δ$AUC $+0.06$ [$+0.03$, $+0.09$], $P=0.001$). In contrast, LLM uncertainty weakly associated with clinical discordance (adjusted OR 1.22 [1.04--1.43], Holm-adjusted $P=0.118$) but provided no incremental discrimination beyond LLM-extracted CCTA stenosis severity ($Δ$AUC $+0.01$ [$-0.00$, $+0.02$], $P=0.245$). Moreover, extraction errors and clinical discordance showed little overlap, with 38 of 42 clinically discordant vessels (90%) having been extracted correctly. LLM uncertainty may identify extraction failures without identifying underlying clinical discordance, supporting failure attribution when evaluating LLM-derived clinical datasets.

title: mFrag: Integrating External DNA Methylation References Improves Lung Cancer Early Detection by Fragmentomics
desc: Fragmentomics analyzes features of circulating cell-free DNA fragments (e.g., fragment length or end motifs) derived from whole-genome sequencing of liquid biopsy samples (blood or other body fluids), enabling non-invasive early cancer detection. Here we present mFrag, a framework that integrates external methylation reference atlases with fragmentomic features for lung cancer detection. mFrag comprises two complementary methods: mFrag-Weight, which uses DNA methylation information to weight fragmentomic features, and mFrag-Net, which integrates fragmentomic features and external DNA methylation data through neural networks. We average the output probabilities of the two methods to obtain a final prediction score. The mFrag model was trained using 287 individuals at risk for lung cancer. In an independent case-control testing set comprising 385 non-cancer controls and 46 cancers (28 stage I, 12 stage II, and 6 stage III or IV), mFrag outperforms a DELFI-style fragmentomic approach, improving PR-AUC from 0.455 to 0.720 and sensitivity at 99% specificity from 0.043 to 0.478, with ROC-AUC from 0.871 to 0.908. For stage I lung cancer, mFrag raises PR-AUC from 0.314 to 0.558 and ROC-AUC from 0.855 to 0.894. Applied to end 4-mer motif features, mFrag likewise improved over an unweighted baseline, with gains contributed by both mFrag-Weight and mFrag-Net. In summary, mFrag improves the accuracy of fragmentomics-based lung cancer detection through integrating external DNA methylation data and the complementarity of its two component models, without incurring any additional data-generating cost.

A Scientific Statement of the ESC Working Group on e-Cardiology, the European Heart Rhythm Association (EHRA), the Association for Acute CardioVascular Care (ACVC), the Heart Failure Association (HFA), the European Association of Cardiovascular Imaging (EACVI), the European Association of Preventive Cardiology (EAPC), and the European Association of Percutaneous Cardiovascular Interventions (EAPCI) of the ESC, the ESC Regulatory Affairs Committee, and the ESC Digital Cardiology and Artificial Intelligence Committee.
source: PubMed · European heart journal. Digital health
desc: [European heart journal. Digital health] Evidence-based medicine represents the systematic approach through which physicians today use the best available scientific evidence from clinical research to guide their clinical decision-making process. However, the emergence of artificial intelligence (AI), with its diverse models and potential applications in medicine, is leading to a new form of research driven by 'big data' and heterogeneous datasets, extending beyond conventional statistical analysis and thereby making AI literacy an increasingly essential competence for clinicians. Artificial intelligence applications in cardiology have shown potential to support disease diagnosis, risk prediction, workflow efficiency, and therapeutic decision-making. However, despite these opportunities, AI may also represent a technological barrier for many physicians, due to its mathematical foundations and the speed at which models evolve. A solid understanding of AI concepts is therefore necessary for cardiologists to critically interpret results and engage with this new research landscape. This scientific statement explores AI in cardiology from an educational perspective, outlining the key knowledge required to build adequate AI literacy. The goal is to enable cardiologists not only to avoid reliance on external experts for methodological decisions, but also to collaborate with greater insight and informed judgment.

title: LLM-Supported Pain Neuroscience Education for Physiotherapy Students
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: İsmail Palalı; conditions: Pain, Chronic Pain, Health Professions Education; type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 120; status: COMPLETED] Physiotherapists need to explain pain to patients in a way that is scientifically accurate, understandable, and non-threatening. Pain neuroscience education (PNE) improves students' pain knowledge, but it is unclear whether this translates into retained ability to explain pain to patients. This randomized controlled trial tested whether adding structured feedback from a large language model (LLM; GPT-5.2 Instant, OpenAI, via the ChatGPT interface) to a standardized four-week PNE programme improves undergraduate physiotherapy students' pain-explanation competence compared with the same programme using standardized expert-developed (non-AI) feedback. The primary outcome was Pain Explanation Competence (PEC) on a previously unseen clinical transfer scenario, assessed without AI access 12 weeks after the intervention by three assessors blinded to group allocation.

title: Accelerometer Data Harmonization and Feature Engineering for Gait Analytics
desc: Gait analytics is utilized for a wide range of health-related applications, ranging from fitness tracking to medical diagnostics, and beyond. Inertial measurement units that are ubiquitously available in mobile devices provide an accessible means of gait analysis but differences in sensor specifications, placement, and recording protocols limit comparability across studies. This study developed and evaluated an analysis-centered data warehouse and standardized quality-assessed processing pipeline to facilitate the integration and joint analysis of heterogeneous gait accelerometer data. Six publicly available datasets including a total of 935 persons were integrated into a star-schema data warehouse, and feature comparability was assessed across datasets and sensor locations. Gender classification served as a proof-of-concept downstream analysis. Gait-cycle extraction, which serves as foundation for feature extraction, was successfully achieved with an accuracy above 99% for the dataset that provides ground truth information. Comparability varied across datasets and sensor configurations, with correlation coefficients between average gait cycles ranging from 0.5 to close to 1.0. Centrally positioned sensors generally show greater correspondence than peripheral sensors, although differences in statistical features persist even between sensors at nominally identical locations. Gender classification performance remains largely near chance level, and no consistent benefit from pooling datasets could be established. These findings demonstrate that heterogeneous gait accelerometer data can be integrated and processed within a common analytical framework, but standardized processing alone does not ensure comparability of the resulting features. The proposed open-source framework implemented in Python provides a foundation for reproducible cross-study gait analysis and for investigating residual heterogeneity associated with datasets and sensor configurations.

title: Adversarial Evaluation of Large Language Models for Patient-Friendly Radiology Report Summarization
desc: Purpose: To develop and validate a scalable adversarial evaluation framework for assessing the robustness of large language models (LLMs) that generate patient-friendly summaries of radiology reports. Methods: We introduced a clinically grounded adversarial framework that uses controlled term substitutions and impression removals across intensity levels. Using a radiologist-validated adversarial dictionary, we generated adversarial variants of CT and MRI reports. Six LLMs summarized original and adversarial impressions using 2 prompt styles, yielding 18,000 evaluation pairs. Robustness was evaluated with an automated LLM-as-a-judge framework scoring factual faithfulness, sensitivity to adversarial edits, certainty fidelity, and hallucination rate. Failure mode analysis quantified vulnerabilities in incorporating clinical modifiers. Agreement with two radiologists was assessed on 105 cases. Results: GPT-5-mini achieved the highest factual faithfulness and certainty fidelity under both adversarial edits. Under term substitution, hallucinations occurred in 28.1-30.1% of GPT-5-mini summaries, compared with 35.3-36.4% for Claude Sonnet 4.5 and 41.4-41.9% for MedGemma. Impression-removal edits were handled more robustly than term substitutions. Even for the highest-scoring summarizer, substitutions of anatomical terms were not reflected in 23.7% of summaries, diagnostic certainty in 22.3%, and descriptor terms (e.g., "substantial") in 21.2%. Judge-radiologist agreement (macro-F1: 0.55-0.56) was comparable to inter-radiologist agreement (0.53). Conclusions: Adversarial evaluation exposes clinically meaningful failure modes, including missed anatomical modifiers, altered diagnostic certainty, and omitted severity descriptors.

title: Realism and resolution: How AI-predicted protein structures differ from experimental structures
desc: Protein structure predictors can recover protein folds with remarkable accuracy, and their models are increasingly used as if they were experimental structures. Yet even for a confidently predicted fold, it remains difficult to judge how faithfully the model reproduces protein geometry. We introduce WhatRes, which assesses a structure from its coordinates on two complementary axes. Apparent resolution estimates the experimental resolution its local geometry most closely resembles. Realism measures how closely that geometry matches experimental structures at the same apparent resolution. Predicted models can score well on apparent resolution while showing systematically less variation in bond lengths and angles than is observed in high-resolution crystal structures. WhatRes reveals this over-idealisation even in high-confidence models.

Artificial Intelligence-Based Modeling to Aid in the Identification of Genetic Conditions in Infants with Congenital Heart Disease.
source: PubMed · medRxiv : the preprint server for health sciences
desc: [medRxiv : the preprint server for health sciences] Genetic conditions are common in congenital heart disease (CHD) and affect care, but are often missed or diagnosed late. We asked whether routine clinical data can shortlist the most likely genetic conditions. Retrospective single-center cohort of children with CHD and an echocardiogram who had either a confirmed genetic diagnosis or negative cytogenetic testing and CHD gene sequencing. Echocardiogram images and serial medical record data were added as model inputs in the order they become clinically available. Class-balanced logistic regression (LR) and a multimodal deep learning fusion network were fitted to the same inputs at each step. The primary metric was balanced top-3 accuracy (correct diagnosis among the top three, averaged across conditions), with bootstrap intervals. The cohort included 1,720 children (988 with common CHD-associated genetic conditions, 231 rare diagnoses, 501 negative testing). Using only inputs generated at the echocardiogram visit, LR reached a balanced top-3 accuracy 0.758 (chance 0.429). Serial records, radiology notes and ICD-10 codes, raised this to 0.809. Multimodal fusion performed similarly at each stage. With a genetic condition withheld from training, the fusion embedding placed affected children nearest to others sharing a gene group in 0.37 of cases versus 0.10 without the embedding (+0.268 [95% CI +0.242, +0.295]). Routine clinical data available at first echocardiogram can help identify likely genetic diagnoses, and later coded inputs ceiling. Multimodal fusion added no accuracy over LR, but places children sharing a genetic cause near one another, making nearest-neighbor retrieval informative for undiagnosed children.

desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Ruijin Hospital; conditions: Pancreas Carcinoma, PDAC - Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma; type: OBSERVATIONAL; enrollment: 50; status: RECRUITING] Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is associated with a poor prognosis, and early detection of pancreatic lesions is of great importance for improving patient outcomes. In this study, whole-body imaging with FDG and FAPI will be used to visualize the early development of pancreatic cancer lesions from multiple perspectives, including glucose metabolism, tumor fibrotic stroma, and integrin receptor expression. Furthermore, leveraging the advantages of four-dimensional dynamic long-axial PET imaging, artificial intelligence-assisted lesion detection and analysis will be performed to characterize lesions and differentiate between benign and malignant lesions. The imaging findings will subsequently be compared with postoperative histopathological results to evaluate the diagnostic performance of the proposed imaging approaches.

title: OPEN: A Community-Informed Metadata Framework for Interoperable Computable Phenotypes
desc: Objective: To identify community - prioritized metadata for reporting and sharing computable phenotypes (CPs), develop a cross-library candidate framework, assess alignment between user requirements and library metadata, and test the feasibility of metadata exchange. Materials and Methods: We combined an international, library - led effort by the Open PhEnomics Network (OPEN) consortium with a UK community consensus-building exercise aimed at improving the FAIRness (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) of CPs. The consortium performed a cross-library field comparison and literature review to inform candidate fields, refined through consortium consensus. The community approach was developed through stakeholder interviews, a survey, and workshop, guided by a working group. Community requirements were interpretively mapped to the resulting framework and classified into conformance tiers. Interoperability was tested by manually and programmatically mapping diabetes-related phenotypes across libraries. Results: The library - led process produced 23 candidate fields spanning phenotype description, data/technical details, and performance domains. Thirteen fields aligned across all five libraries, and 22 fields aligned with published CP library desiderata. Interoperability testing successfully catalogued phenotypes through manual mapping, with API - mediated mapping achieving 63 - 76% metadata field completeness across libraries. A community survey (n=124 respondents) identified six metadata elements with majority support as mandatory: description, coding terminology, phenotype type, version history, unique identifier, and data source. Logic representation and validation requirements were rated as mostly context-dependent. Community - identified priorities showed strong alignment with the OPEN framework, though some requirements were only partially represented. Discussion: Through a consensus - based, community - driven approach, we established a CP framework enabling interoperability across libraries. Conclusion: OPEN provides a credible, community - informed foundation for a FAIR CP metadata standard.

title: Health-System-Wide Mapping of Demographic Information in Routine Clinical Histopathology
desc: The extent to which demographic-associated information is detectable across organs and disease states in routine clinical histopathology remains unclear. Here, we analyzed 1.3 million hematoxylin and eosin whole-slide images from 257,322 patients across 25 organs, using pathology foundation-model representations and multiple-instance learning to systematically map information associated with sex, age group, and self-reported race. Across 69 organ-demographic combinations, demographic attributes were broadly recoverable, with pan-organ mean AUROCs of 0.828 for sex, 0.733 for age group, and 0.662 for self-reported race, and substantial variation across organs. Demographic-class balancing produced relatively small changes in performance, while evaluation within diagnosis-text clusters showed modest attenuation. Under training with diagnosis-based grouping, demographic-associated signals remained detectable across multiple organs, including sex in gastric tissue (AUROC 0.865), age group in breast (0.816), and self-reported race in skin (0.728). Literature-guided analysis of these settings generated candidate histomorphological and contextual explanations for further investigation. Together, these findings provide a systematic map of demographic-associated information in routine histopathology, informing investigations of its sources, assessments of potential shortcut learning, and the development of more interpretable computational pathology models.

title: Rapid generation of antibody conformational ensembles using machine learning
desc: We introduce Cadense, a generative framework for antibody ensemble prediction that produces diverse Fv structures from sequence, informed by conformational dynamics. While a valuable resource, static structure prediction provides only a single snapshot of dynamic proteins, whose motions influence their binding and other properties. This is particularly relevant for antibodies, an important class of molecules for drug discovery, where flexible complementarity determining region (CDR) loops are difficult to model with static approaches. Cadense addresses this gap by generating ensembles that match conformational and biophysical property distributions from molecular dynamics (MD), while reducing the computational burden from days of simulation to seconds of generation. We show Cadense ensembles can recover both apo and holo conformations of the same antibody and serve as effective input to physics-based docking, capturing the conformational flexibility important to properly model antibody antigen interactions. Together, these results establish Cadense as a useful tool for antibody conformational ensemble generation with the promise to enable faster, dynamics-aware antibody design.

Artificial intelligence triages chest radiographs: Optimising diagnostic workflow efficiency in hospital settings.
desc: [Radiography (London, England : 1995)] This narrative review assesses the impact of artificial intelligence (AI)-driven chest radiograph (CXR) triage on the efficiency and accuracy of diagnostic workflows in hospital radiology departments. It includes regulatory-approved CXR triage software introduced since 2021 and evaluates key metrics such as sensitivity and report turnaround time in both real-world and simulated clinical environments. Twelve peer-reviewed studies, including single-centre and multicentre investigations across nine countries, were synthesised. AI-driven CXR triage detected selected critical abnormalities and prioritised urgent cases, with reductions in report turnaround time reported across workflow simulations, retrospective evaluations, prospective studies, and one large randomised controlled trial. However, evidence of improved downstream diagnosis or patient outcomes remains limited. Current evidence supports the potential clinical value of AI-driven CXR triage as adjuncts to radiologists and radiographers in hospital settings, demonstrating meaningful improvements in diagnostic efficiency and workflow performance. Continued large-scale, real-world validation, alongside attention to ethical, educational, and integration factors, is needed to support safe and sustainable adoption in radiographic practice. The findings of this review offer valuable insights to inform clinical workflows in hospitals worldwide, particularly those managing substantial CXR caseloads. AI-driven CXR triage should support the interpretation by reporting practitioners. Safe implementation requires local validation, integration with existing workflows, clear governance, staff education, and ongoing monitoring of diagnostic accuracy, reporting efficiency, and downstream patient outcomes. Because faster reporting does not necessarily accelerate diagnosis or treatment, adoption should be supported by coordinated pathway redesign and continued human oversight.

title: Effect of AI-Assisted Hand Hygiene Training on Hand Hygiene Competency in Newly Hired Workers
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Sir Run Run Shaw Hospital; conditions: Healthy Adult Participants; type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 260; status: COMPLETED] The goal of this clinical trial is to learn if artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted training works better than usual training. The training aims to improve handwashing skill in newly hired healthcare workers. The AI-assisted training uses a screen that shows feedback right away. The main questions it aims to answer are: Does AI-assisted training lead to higher overall handwashing skill scores than usual training? Does AI-assisted training improve harder handwashing steps? These include interlaced fingers, locked fingers, and fingertip rubbing. Researchers will compare AI-assisted training to usual instructor-led training. They will see if AI-assisted training improves handwashing skill. Participants will: Attend a 30-minute class on the World Health Organization (WHO) seven-step handwashing method. The class also explains how the skill test works. Be assigned by chance to usual training or AI-assisted training. Both trainings last 45 minutes. In the AI-assisted group, use a camera and screen. The screen shows their hand movements and gives feedback right away. This helps them correct their movements. Take a final handwashing skill test. The same AI system scores 12 parts of the WHO seven-step method. Two hundred sixty newly hired healthcare workers joined this study at one hospital in China. They included doctors, nurses, research staff, lab staff, and support staff.

title: Task-adaptive anonymisation enables privacy-preserving sharing of clinical speech data
desc: Clinical speech is increasingly used for disease screening and clinical assessment, but directly distributing speech recordings poses privacy risks because they contain both speaker-identifying voiceprints and sensitive spoken content. Existing speech anonymisation approaches are primarily developed for general speech applications or task-specific clinical speech and overlook that different clinical tasks rely on distinct speech characteristics, necessitating task-adaptive anonymisation strategies to protect patient privacy while preserving clinical utility. Here we introduce CASA, a clinically adaptive speech anonymisation agent that transforms anonymisation from a fixed processing procedure into a task-guided optimisation process, dynamically tailoring voiceprint and content anonymisation to task-specific privacy and clinical utility requirements. Through recursive self-improvement (RSI), CASA iteratively evaluates and refines anonymisation strategies against task-specific privacy and clinical utility requirements, while learning from these outcomes to guide more efficient planning in subsequent clinical tasks. CASA is validated across 14 clinical tasks encompassing five languages, diverse elicitation paradigms, and mental health, cognitive and voice disorders. CASA preserved disease-related classification performance while meeting speaker-anonymisation requirements across all clinical tasks, versus only 8/14 for the strongest fixed method. Assessments of resistance to speaker re-identification by external attackers and identification and redaction of sensitive personal information in clinical speech further demonstrated CASA's dual protection of speaker identity and sensitive spoken content. Clinical expert assessments further supported the preservation of clinically relevant information and the acceptability of anonymised speech for controlled research sharing.

title: GeneEmbedLLM: Harnessing Large Language Models for Gene Functional Embedding and Association Prediction
desc: Effective and high-quality gene function representations are crucial for bioinformatics tasks. While biological knowledge about genes is inherently textual, encompassing functional descriptions and pathway annotations, current methods often rely on single-source, non-textual data, failing to capture the rich semantic information in multi-source gene annotations. In this paper, we propose GeneEmbedLLM, a Large Language Model (LLM)-powered framework for generating universal, semantically-aware gene embeddings. The proposed approach advances the gene representation learning through multi-source structured text integration from five authoritative databases and attribute-aware attention based on Longformer architecture and contrastive learning. Experimental results on diverse downstream tasks, ranging from molecular interactions and phenotypic dependencies to epigenetic regulation, confirm the validity and effectiveness of our proposed approach, where competitive performance is achieved across all evaluated benchmarks. We further validate the quality of the generated embeddings through comprehensive analyses, including embedding visualizations, intra-pathway similarity assessments, ablation study, and parameter analysis.
